item.title: Unveiling plastic rearrangements in silica glass through persistent homology
item.description: arXiv:2611.26970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plastic deformation of amorphous solids proceeds through localised atomic rearrangements. While much effort has been devoted to identifying where such rearrangements occur, how the local structure changes during a rearrangement is less well understood. In silica glass, a rearrangement can involve both distortion within SiO4 tetrahedra and deformation of the network connecting them, but the contributions of these two modes have rarely been quantified. Here, we characterise plastic rearrangements in silica glass under athermal quasistatic shear using persistent homology, which extracts rings from atomic configurations, and link the changes in the persistence diagrams to individual rings in real space. We classify rearrangement events into two types according to bond-coordination changes. By performing inverse analysis, we reveal that Si-centred triangles within tetrahedra, hinge triangles spanning two corner-sharing tetrahedra, and the other (non-hinge) O3 triangles are the dominant sources of topological changes upon rearrangements. The birth-time changes of Si-centred and hinge triangles closely follow the change in the angle opposite the longest edge, whereas that of non-hinge triangles also reflects changes in inter-tetrahedral O--O distances. Further, we clarify that triangles with large birth-time changes are localised in the rearrangement region. Comparing the two types of triangles, we find that the ratio of their birth-time changes is larger for coordination-changing events than for coordination-preserving events, indicating that such events involve relatively more intra-tetrahedral deformation compared with network deformation. These results demonstrate that persistent homology separates intra-tetrahedral and network deformation and quantifies each as a continuous quantity within a single framework.
item.dc:creator: Fuya Katsuyama, Kumpei Shiraishi, Emi Minamitani

item.title: Ultraslow vorticity modes in colloidal fluids
item.description: arXiv:2611.27172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the conventional unsteady-Stokes picture, vorticity generated by a transient disturbance relaxes rapidly through viscous diffusion once the forcing ceases. This view presumes a quiescent solvent. In colloidal and biological fluids, thermal motion continually perturbs the surrounding fluid, raising a natural question: can equilibrium fluctuations, mediated by hydrodynamic coupling, sustain vorticity over mesoscopic scales and times? Here, using high-speed confocal microscopy of moderately dense colloidal suspensions, we reconstruct the conditional mean hydrodynamic response to Brownian displacements of prescribed magnitude and direction. We find a long-lived, spatially structured vorticity field that decays far more slowly than predicted by unforced unsteady-Stokes dynamics. A coarse-grained phenomenological model based on fractional Brownian motion, constrained by independently measured single-particle subdiffusion, quantitatively captures its temporal and spatial decay. These findings reveal a field-level manifestation of hydrodynamic memory in fluctuating low-Reynolds-number flows, with implications for transport and collective dynamics in complex fluids.
item.dc:creator: Satyam Raheja, Noman Hanif Barbhuiya, Tsvi Tlusty, Chandan K. Mishra

item.title: Recoverable Necking Enabled by Reverse Phase-Boundary Motion in Liquid Crystal Elastomers
item.description: arXiv:2611.27194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strain localization is often associated with plastic flow and permanent deformation. Here we show that a tensile neck in a crosslinked nematic network can undergo nearly complete recovery through reverse phase-boundary motion, leaving little residual deformation. In a monodomain liquid crystal elastomer stretched perpendicular to its initial director, this recovery occurs during an isothermal loading-unloading cycle. Digital image correlation resolves the process as the retreat of interfaces separating low- and high-stretch regions, where the high-stretch domain shrinks while previously necked material thickens, despite substantial mechanical hysteresis. Within the recoverable-necking regime, increasing temperature lowers the loading plateau stress but raises the unloading plateau stress. A nonconvex constitutive description provides an energetic basis for the coexistence of the two stretch states, while gradient regularization accounts for the finite width of their interfaces through an equilibrium reference profile. These results identify the spatial mechanism of neck recovery and distinguish recoverable strain localization from mechanical reversibility in an orientationally ordered polymer network.
item.dc:creator: Weida Kang, Yufeng Zhang, Changyue Liu, Zhijian Wang, Xudong Liang

item.title: Revealing the growth of structural length in glass-forming liquids without using dynamical information
item.description: arXiv:2611.27231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical heterogeneity underlies the dramatic slowdown of supercooled liquids and has long been a central topic in glass physics. Despite considerable progress in identifying structural motifs and order parameters correlated with dynamical heterogeneity, a general characterization of structural descriptors remains elusive because they can vary among glass formers and are not generally known \emph{a priori}. To address this challenge, we establish a unified framework that can be applied to varieties of glass formers to extract structural signatures of dynamical heterogeneity directly from their static configurations. The framework combines a graph neural network (GNN) with gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Across three canonical three-dimensional glass-forming models, the resulting structural field exhibits a characteristic correlation length that tracks the corresponding dynamical correlation length. Notably, a network trained on small systems can be applied to larger systems without retraining, indicating that the extracted features are encoded in local and mesoscopic structural correlations. These results demonstrate that static configurations encode structural signatures of dynamical heterogeneity and establish a scalable, interpretable route for extracting them.
item.dc:creator: Min Liu, Daisuke Nishigaito, Yusuke Hara, Norihiro Oyama, Takeshi Kawasaki

item.title: Decoupling Entropic and Enthalpic Elasticity in Crosslinked Polymer Nanocomposites
item.description: arXiv:2611.27259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanoparticle-induced local interface regions significantly enhance the bulk mechanical behavior of polymer nanocomposites, yet their energetic contribution in crosslinked elastomer networks remains poorly understood. Here, we decouple the entropic and enthalpic contributions to the elasticity of crosslinked poly(dimethylsiloxane) nanocomposites using temperature-dependent thermomechanical measurements. While the measured bulk elastic modulus exhibits a monotonic increase with nanoparticle volume fraction $\phi_{\rm n}$, we observe that the effective crosslink density initially increases before saturating at larger $\phi_{\rm n}$. These results are independently validated across two nanoparticle systems (silica and titania) and directly confirmed by X-ray scattering experiments on silica-based composites, highlighting the generality of the observation. The trends in effective crosslink density indicate that the elastic response is predominantly entropy-driven at low nanoparticle concentrations, whereas enthalpic contributions become increasingly significant at higher loadings. Assuming a linear superposition of interface and bulk contributions, these results reveal that the effective crosslink density at the particle interface decreases by an order of magnitude below a critical mean interparticle separation, indicating that localized particle proximity and clustering constrain the entropic elasticity at higher loadings.
item.dc:creator: Chiranjit Majhi, Sivasurender Chandran, Krishnacharya Khare

item.title: Optimizing MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with burst-mode free-electron laser operation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Burst-mode X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide a powerful platform for X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments with sub-microsecond temporal resolution, but the achievable performance is constrained in practice by both photon statistics and the sample's dose tolerance. Here, we develop an analytical framework for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of pulsed XPCS measurements, including pulse-to-pulse fluctuations of the incident intensity. We combine this description with dose constraints and show that, for a fixed maximum dose, acquiring fewer frames at higher per-pulse intensity yields a higher SNR than distributing the dose over a larger number of low-intensity frames. The framework is validated against measurements at the European XFEL, where the intensity fluctuations of the investigated operation mode are found to cause only a negligible reduction in SNR. We further introduce and experimentally demonstrate a rolling bunch pattern with three pulses per train and variable pulse spacings. This scheme enables more than an order-of-magnitude increase in the accessible per-pulse intensity while maintaining equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide practical guidelines for optimizing dose-efficient MHz-XPCS experiments and for evaluating future XFEL operation modes.
item.dc:creator: Johannes M\"oller, Wonhyuk Jo, Trey Guest, Lars Fr\"ohlich, Matthias Scholz, Marc Guetg, Felix Brau{\ss}e, Aliaksandr Leonau, James Wrigley, Ulrike Boesenberg, Lea Brings, J\"org Hallmann, Jan-Etienne Pudell, Angel Rodriguez-Fernandez, Roman Shayduk, Alexey Zozulya, Nimmi Das Anthuparambil, Michelle Dargasz, Sonja Timmermann, Maddalena Bin, Foivos Perakis, Michael Paulus, Felix Lehmk\"uhler, Christian Gutt, Anders Madsen

item.title: Saddle Buckling of a Multicellular Alga Driven by Differential Growth
item.description: arXiv:2611.27563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: During development of many simple multicellular organisms there is a complex interplay between cell growth and generation of an extracellular matrix that confers structure. We study this problem quantitatively using $Gonium~pectorale$, a 16-cell alga that transforms from a flat to a buckled shape during growth without cell division or rearrangement. Cell-level measurements and 3D reconstructions show that the $12$ peripheral cells grow faster than the central $4$, producing hoop stress that selects the saddle mode, whose amplitude displays a continuous bifurcation with classical square root singularity. These results are consistent with a continuum model of differential growth within F\"oppl--von K\'arm\'an theory, which yields information on the mechanical properties of the ECM. Implications of this transformation in evolutionary transitions to multicellularity are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Wang, Sumit Kumar Birwa, Jane Y. Y. Chui, Kyriacos Leptos, Raymond E. Goldstein

item.title: Lacrymaria-like dynamics: compression and length change in active slender bodies
item.description: arXiv:2611.27577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Length change is central to the behaviour of many active slender bodies, yet most elastohydrodynamic models of microscopic locomotion treat filaments as effectively inextensible. Here we introduce a compressible $N$-link formulation for planar active filaments, in which both bending angles and segment lengths are dynamical variables coupled through local hydrodynamic drag, modelled using resistive force theory. We first use the model to test whether passive extensibility can improve bending-driven swimming and crawling. Across the parameter ranges studied, passive compressibility usually reduces locomotion speed, indicating that axial compliance alone is not a robust mechanism for propulsion enhancement. We then prescribe active rest-length waves and show that compression can either enhance, suppress, or redirect locomotion depending on its phase, wavelength, and frequency relative to bending. Finally, motivated by the extensible neck dynamics of \textit{Lacrymaria olor}, we apply the method to clamped and free filaments driven by oscillatory follower forces. These examples show that elastic compression-bending coupling can reorganise swimming, exploration, and locomotion in strongly deforming active filaments.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Moreau, Yukinori Nishigami, Johann H\'erault, Kenta Ishimoto

item.title: Disentangling Lengthscales in Disordered Fracture
item.description: arXiv:2611.27581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The interplay between quenched disorder and collective interactions can generate multiple emergent lengthscales in damage processes, yet their roles in determining the strength of heterogeneous materials remain incompletely understood. Here, we develop a coarse-grained description of load redistribution in the two-dimensional random fuse model (RFM) with Weibull-distributed quenched disorder, interpreting shielding in the crack-tip damage density as a consequence of nonlocal current redistribution. Our numerical results distinguish this emergent screening length, identified as the size of the statistical fracture process zone, from the regularizing length in Bazant's established quasibrittle size-effect law (SEL), revealing their distinct disorder dependences, and challenging previous associations of the two. We further uncover a comparable scaling between the SEL and pre-failure crack extension, suggesting the former may instead be more naturally associated with a percolation process of micro-fractures around the crack-tip. These findings disentangle important emergent lengthscales within the RFM, and highlight a candidate physical mechanism for explaining macroscopic size effects in quasibrittle fracture.
item.dc:creator: Matthaios Chouzouris, Marcelo A. Dias

item.title: Capillary partitioning of solutes on conformally coated colloidal monolayers: a universal geometric threshold
item.description: arXiv:2611.27658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Depositing a conformal solid film on a hexagonal monolayer of spheres progressively closes the interstitial pores, and this closure controls where a dilute solute spin-coated from a volatile solvent ends up after drying: buried in the interstitial valleys or spread over the exposed caps. We derive the fraction of solute that ends in the valleys from first principles, for any sphere radius, film thickness and wetting liquid. The control parameter is the film thickness divided by the sphere radius, and a purely geometric threshold, about 0.155, separates two regimes for all sphere sizes. Below it, the three-sphere interstice is an open cup that the liquid fills through a narrow throat at the sphere equator, and about nine tenths of the solute end in the valleys. Above it, the throat pinches shut, sealing the cup and leaving only a shallow surface dimple, so this fraction drops more than twofold, never to recover. Treating the throat as a nearly triangular duct gives a closed-form filling rate, confirmed by exact flow calculations. During spin-coating, filling outpaces drying by up to five orders of magnitude, except within a fraction of a nanometre of the threshold. Partitioning is therefore set by capacity alone, through a one-parameter ratio of exact void volumes, identical for all sphere sizes. Thin-film simulations confirm the direction of liquid transport. For dye in ethanol on tantalum-pentoxide-coated polystyrene lattices, the predicted on-cap fraction rises from 0.06 to 0.76 across the threshold, agreeing at both ends with values inferred from measured Purcell factors.
item.dc:creator: Renaud A. L. Vall\'ee, Carlos Drummond

item.title: Silver/alumina-capped Janus particles: a dispersible hyperbolic metamaterial
item.description: arXiv:2611.27736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperbolic metamaterials (HMMs) made of alternating layers of metal and dielectric have been heralded as promising materials for super-resolution imaging and spontaneous emission enhancement sought after in biological applications. However, the practical utilization of HMMs has been limited, primarily by the solid and stiff nature of the underlying substrate, usually a silicon wafer or glass substrate. An ability to transfer HMMs to colloidal substrates would introduce dispersibility to HMMs and potentially enable their use in medical applications while extending the curved HMM geometry to discrete particles. Here, spherical particles with alternating metal and dielectric layers are used to fabricate hyperbolic metamaterial-capped Janus particles (HMMJPs). Alternating layers of silver (metal) and alumina (dielectric) films are evaporated onto polystyrene particle monolayers with and without fluorescent properties to study the impact of particle curvature on the layer structure in the cap. The thickness and number of layers are chosen such that the final cap film resembles the structure of a 4P-HMM film, four periods of alternating silver/alumina, previously characterized as an HMM at wavelengths above 403 nm. The fluorescent character of the polystyrene particles is used to illuminate the pathway of light in the HMMJP clusters as a function of cluster size and geometry. Subsequently, resonance imaging microscopy (RIM) with the HaloElement is used to independently verify the HMM nature of a single HMMJP.
item.dc:creator: Samhita Kattekola, Raymond R. Dagastine, Alexander Couzis, Ilona Kretzschmar

item.title: Corrections to the Fick-Jacobs Description of Diffusion across Pickering Droplet Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.27818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Particle-laden interfaces give rise to important classes of multiphase materials, including Pickering-Ramsden systems and bicontinuous interfacially jammed emulsion gels (bijels). In these systems, colloidal particles adsorb at fluid-fluid interfaces and form semipermeable layers that provide structural stability and controlled diffusive transport. These properties make them attractive for encapsulation applications and motivate understanding transport across particle-laden interfaces. Diffusion through geometries with varying cross-section, including those found at particle-laden interfaces, is commonly described using the Fick-Jacobs formalism. However, this approach relies on the assumptions of slowly varying geometries and rapid equilibration in the transverse direction. Subsequent studies have developed corrections based on higher-order geometric derivatives, but an elegant closed-form description remains elusive. Here, we compare predictions of the Fick-Jacobs model with fully resolved simulations of 2D Pickering droplets. We find that discrepancies in model predictions increase with interfacial particle crowding, revealing the limits of the Fick-Jacobs approximation. We show that the required correction can be understood through simple geometrical arguments. Our results provide an effective framework for describing transport across particle-laden interfaces and lay the foundation for a more general description of diffusion in complex geometries.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Khandoori, Wim Thielemans, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Shear thinning confines the wall forcing: laminar chaotic mixing of Carreau fluids in a rotating arc-wall mixer
item.description: arXiv:2611.27150v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With two-dimensional simulations of Carreau fluids of power-law index $N$ from 1 to 0.4, I study how shear thinning modifies laminar chaotic mixing in an open channel stirred by three arc-shaped wall segments rotating back and forth periodically, the upper one in anti-phase with the two lower ones. The outlet mixing efficiency falls monotonically, by 14 percent from $N=1$ to 0.4, mostly between $N=0.85$ and 0.6. The bulk flow and its chaotic saddle are nearly unaffected. Shear thinning acts instead through a thin layer of reduced viscosity around the moving arcs: the geometric penetration length of the wall forcing shortens as the 0.3 power of the time-mean wall viscosity, within 4 percent over a fourfold range of forcing. This confinement weakens the stretching, and the penetration length predicts the mixing efficiency ($r^2=0.97$). The optimal Strouhal number stays close to 0.7 for all fluids, but shear thinning narrows the range of efficient periods. A lamellar model indicates that the relative penalty of shear thinning grows with the Peclet number. As the injected power scales with the wall viscosity, the mixing efficiency per unit energy rises 2.6-fold from $N=1$ to 0.4, and at equal energy per unit volume, with a faster rotation, the fluid with $N=0.4$ mixes as well as the Newtonian one, and better at larger energies. In wall-driven mixers, the reach of the forcing, not the bulk viscosity, is the quantity to control.
item.dc:creator: Teodor Burghelea

item.title: Emergent Fourfold Symmetry in Polarization Images: Local Origin and Diffractive Breakdown
item.description: arXiv:2611.27452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A polarization image can gain or lose rotational symmetry with no change in material symmetry. In axisymmetric anisotropic systems, covariance restricts the field to azimuthal orders $m=0,\pm2$, guaranteeing twofold but not fourfold symmetry; pointwise unitarity adds fourfold symmetry, which diffraction can destroy. Holographic Jones fields of liquid-crystal torons show propagation shifts the twofold--fourfold balance; for the same director, a marching-wave model qualitatively reproduces the twofold morphology missed by a local model. This establishes a symmetry hierarchy for polarization imaging.

item.title: A nonlinear transient finite element analysis of coupled solvent diffusion and large deformation of magneto-elastic hydrogel balloon
item.description: arXiv:2611.27644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates the transient swelling of an initially spherical magnetoelastic hydrogel balloon. The balloon is inflated at constant internal pressure and exposed to the non-uniform magnetic field of one or two current-carrying coils. The gel is modelled as a compressible Ogden network mixed with solvent through Flory--Huggins theory, with an additive elastic--mixing--magnetic decomposition of the free energy. A fully coupled nonlinear finite element formulation uses a staggered solution scheme and a Taylor--Hood-type discretisation. It follows the balloon from its dry inflated state to either swollen equilibrium or burst. The formulation recovers the analytical free-swelling stretch and the delayed-burst regime, and its converged states agree with equilibrium energy minimisation. Symmetry-breaking (pear-shaped) dry configurations do not survive swelling: they rearrange rapidly and then relax by diffusion onto the symmetric branch. Transient membrane stresses can exceed their equilibrium values by nearly an order of magnitude. For coils which are sufficiently close to undeformed balloon, fields beyond a critical intensity close the slow-inflation curve into a loop. Stable swollen equilibria then exist only within a bounded pressure window that narrows as the field increases, and outside of it the balloon bursts. Under two coaxial coils, asymmetry about the equator appears only when the coils differ in current or radius. The magnetic field therefore acts as a control parameter for shape of balloon and permits or prevents stable swelling at a given pressure.
item.dc:creator: Nadeem Karim Shaikh, Ganesh Tamadapu

item.title: Cyclic perturbations encode memories in trained neural networks without loss of performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.27647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many disordered materials exhibit a remarkable form of memory: they retain information about the history of cyclic perturbations. Whether this phenomenon also occurs in artificial neural networks, whose mathematical structure and dynamics share many similarities with disordered physical systems, is unknown. Here we show that cyclically perturbing a trained, overparameterized deep neural network encodes information in the structure of the weights that can subsequently be retrieved, thus retaining memory of the perturbation history. During each write cycle, all weights are displaced, after which the network relaxes through gradient descent. Repeated cycles organise the neural network into a state that is reversible for perturbations up to the write amplitude, allowing the encoded value to be read from the onset of irreversible weight motion. Multiple memories can also be encoded, although under deterministic writing only the largest persists at long times. Inspired by cyclically sheared suspensions, we introduce a novel noisy-write protocol that preserves all encoded memories at long times. Remarkably, neither deterministic nor noisy memory writing measurably affects the network's performance on unseen data from its original learning task. Our results establish cyclic memory as a phenomenon shared by disordered physical systems and deep neural networks, and show that networks can exploit as yet unexplored memory capabilities without compromising their original function.
item.dc:creator: Max Kerr Winter, Liesbeth M. C. Janssen

item.title: Minkowski Correlation Functions (MCF): Long-range, robust shape descriptors for point patterns
item.description: arXiv:2611.27948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A morphometric analysis of point patterns using Minkowski functionals is short-sighted, whereas correlation functions do not provide robust, i.e., additive shape descriptors. To combine the advantages of both standard techniques and to overcome their weaknesses, we introduce ring-based Minkowski correlation functions (MCFs) as robust and sensitive descriptors of disordered point patterns. By assigning to each point a spherical shell and quantifying the resulting two-phase morphology via Minkowski functionals, MCFs capture structural information across multiple length scales, remain sensitive at radii where conventional disk-based Minkowski functionals have saturated, and implicitly encode higher-order correlations beyond the pair correlation and structure factor. We present an exact and efficient algorithm for planar patterns extending the established disk-based morphological approach to long ranges. Applications across scales -- active colloids (Quincke rollers), longleaf pine trees, and the Hubble Ultra Deep Field -- demonstrate clear and systematic deviations from homogeneous Poisson references, with distinct responses of covered area, boundary length, and Euler characteristic. The approach combines short computation times, robustness to noise, and straightforward edge handling with clear interpretability as low-dimensional functions of the outer ring radius.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Pabst, Michael A. Klatt, Klaus Mecke

item.title: Molecular structure breaks universality in screening behavior of electrolyte solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.27955v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrostatic screening is one of the most fundamental phenomena in electrolyte solutions. While dilute electrolytes are described by the universal Debye--H\"uckel theory, recent experiments have reported an apparently universal scaling law for screening lengths in concentrated electrolytes, fueling ongoing debate over anomalous underscreening. Yet, liquid state theory has been unable to determine whether molecular details of the solvent, the ions, or both should preserve or break such universality. Using machine-learned classical density functional theory, we compute numerically exact decay lengths across a hierarchy of electrolyte models of increasing molecular complexity. We find that molecular details qualitatively reshape screening: solvent attraction generates a new monotonic decay mode, solvent polarity produces re-entrant behavior, and ionic structure alone can drastically alter screening-length exponents. Consequently, no single scaling law describes screening universally across these molecularly distinct electrolytes. Our results challenge equilibrium interpretations of experimentally observed universality in concentrated electrolytes.
item.dc:creator: Anna T. Bui, Connie J. Fairchild, Dominic P. W. Thomas, Stephen J. Cox

item.title: Receptor Abundance Alone Underpredicts Red Blood Cell Adhesion in Gaucher Disease
item.description: arXiv:2611.27960v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) in Gaucher disease (GD) adhere abnormally to vessel walls and carry more Lutheran/basal cell adhesion molecule (Lu/BCAM), a laminin receptor. Whether receptor abundance sets this adhesion is untested. We simulated RBCs carrying stochastic Lu/BCAM-laminin bonds, calibrated a population on control donors, and predicted GD adhesion from the 1.3-fold receptor rise. On laminin and endothelium the data exceed the prediction 1.6- to 1.7-fold. Matching them requires 2.4- and 4.6-fold more binding-competent receptors, compatible with the estimated 5.7-fold rise in phosphorylated receptors. Neither a stiffer membrane nor higher bond affinity removes the shortfall at high shear stress. In sickle cell disease, given active-receptor counts, the model predicts the fall in adhesion under hydroxyurea within 1.4-fold, while total receptors rise. Adhesion likely follows receptor state more than abundance. Stiffening instead retains cells at a splenic slit.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Pierre A. Buffet, Melanie Franco, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: A unified geometric design framework for kirigami structures
item.description: arXiv:2608.30032v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kirigami turns a thin sheet with cuts into a shape-morphing mechanical metamaterial, with applications across science and engineering. While various two- and three-dimensional kirigami design methods have been developed, most of them are only applicable to a limited class of kirigami structures. In this work, we present a unified geometric design framework for kirigami structures. Since the states of a kirigami pattern differ only in which tile corners coincide, one tessellation routine generates them all, and edge-length equalities couple them. A single constrained optimization then designs 2D-to-2D, 2D-to-3D, and 3D-to-3D shape-morphing, compact reconfigurable, and rigidly deployable structures, and one sheet that deploys into two prescribed shapes. The designs further reveal geometric laws hidden in the kirigami mechanism, which explain how reconfiguration transposes the shape of a sheet, how one sheet bends into both a bowl and a saddle, and why the outline of a flat sheet limits the curvature it can reach when it closes again. Altogether, our work paves a new way for the design of shape-morphing mechanical metamaterials.
item.dc:creator: Qinghai Jiang, Gary P. T. Choi

item.title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
item.description: arXiv:2610.26688v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that the director can rotate at no cost of free energy when accompanied by a corresponding stress-free, ground-state deformation. The resulting neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE, when minimized over the director, is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.
item.dc:creator: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai

item.title: Three-dimensional photon transport in spinodal photocatalytic aerogels: how bicontinuous morphology controls kinetic rate constants
item.description: arXiv:2604.13929v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anatase TiO2 dispersed in a silica aerogel matrix forms porous monolithic photocatalysts promising for indoor air purification and VOC photo-degradation. Their bicontinuous spinodal architecture provides high surface area, structural integrity, and intense UV multiple scattering. Extracting kinetic descriptors from apparent rate constants requires an optical model for the photon fluence, and current practice replaces the 3D pore network by a homogeneous 1D slab with effective optical coefficients -- an approximation never quantified for spinodal geometries. We combine realistic 3D spinodal pore masks from Cahn-Hilliard spectral integration with 3D GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo (MC) photon-migration simulations, introducing the solid-phase-weighted estimator $\Phi_{3D}$ and comparing it with the conventional volume average $\Phi_{1D}$ and the diffusion-approximation (DA) prediction $\Phi_{DA}$. The ratio $\Phi_{3D}/\Phi_{1D}$ equals 1.515 at porosity $\phi=0.70$ and 1.774 at $\phi=0.90$: the solid phase is preferentially illuminated, traced to optical phase contrast. Since pores neither absorb nor scatter, photons cross quasi-ballistically, and the void phase sustains only $r=0.514$ of the solid-phase fluence, diluting the volume average with dark voxels. This ratio is porosity-independent, so the concentration ratio obeys the exact relation $1/[\phi r+(1-\phi)]$, reproducing both simulated values. The kinetic descriptor $k_{surf}\cdot K_{ads}$ is underestimated by 20% via the DA route and overestimated by 51.5% via the volume-averaged route. Homogeneous-slab MC simulations at matched optical thickness show that 84% of the fluence-weighted RMS discrepancy between MC and DA is intrinsic to the bicontinuous architecture and beyond any effective-medium DA. These results give a quantitative correction for kinetic extraction and design rules linking porosity, pore size and photon utilisation.
item.dc:creator: Renaud A. L. Vall\'ee
